title: SEO Guide for B2B: 2026 Strategy for Leads and Revenue
summary: Our SEO Guide for B2B shows how to build strategy, map intent, create converting content, fix tech SEO, and track ROI in 2026. Drive leads and revenue.
body_text: Welcome to your complete SEO guide for B2B. In the world of business to business marketing, your buyers are researchers. A staggering 71% of them begin their purchasing journey with a simple Google search. They aren’t just looking for products; they’re looking for solutions, expertise, and trustworthy partners. If your business isn’t showing up, you’re invisible. This guide breaks down everything you need to build a powerful B2B SEO strategy that doesn’t just attract traffic, it drives qualified leads and fuels growth. We’ll cover everything from foundational planning and content creation to technical tune ups and measuring what matters. B2B SEO Strategy 2026: The Bottom Line To win in 2026, B2B SEO must evolve into Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) . This involves shifting from high-volume keywords to high-intent long-tail queries and optimizing for AI Overviews. Successful strategies focus on three pillars: E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trust), Topic Authority through content clusters, and Technical Precision to ensure AI models can crawl and cite your data as a primary source. Part 1: Building Your B2B SEO Foundation Success in SEO starts with a solid plan. Before you write a single blog post, you need to understand who you’re talking to and what they’re looking for. This is the strategic core of any effective SEO guide for B2B. Define Your B2B SaaS SEO Strategy A B2B SaaS SEO strategy is a specific plan designed for software companies with long sales cycles and niche audiences. The goal isn’t just traffic; it’s attracting qualified leads who are actively researching solutions to their business problems. This is critical because 85% of B2B decision makers trust organic search results more than paid ads. A strong organic presence builds immediate credibility. Your strategy should focus on creating content that addresses specific pain points, targets technical keywords, and guides users through a complex buyer journey. Identify Your Target Audience First, you need to know exactly who you’re trying to reach. Target audience identification is the process of defining the specific group of professionals you want as customers. What are their job titles, industries, and company sizes? What challenges keep them up at night? Getting this right ensures your entire strategy, from the keywords you choose to the tone of your content, resonates with the people most likely to buy from you. Comparison: B2B vs. B2C SEO Objectives Feature B2B SEO Focus B2C SEO Focus Primary Goal Lead Quality & Pipeline Transaction Volume Sales Cycle Long (4–12 months) Short (Minutes–Days) Content Type Technical, Visionary, ROI-focused Emotional, Trend-based, Urgent Decision Maker Buying Committee (6–10 people) Individual Consumer AI Visibility Citation in Research-heavy AIOs Quick Product Comparisons Develop Detailed Buyer Personas Once you know your audience, bring them to life with buyer personas. These are semi fictional profiles of your ideal customers. A great persona includes details like job responsibilities, goals, pain points, and the types of questions they ask Google. This process is worth its weight in gold. In fact, 71% of companies that exceed their revenue goals have documented buyer personas. Why? Because personas transform your marketing from company focused to customer centric, making your website and content far more effective for your target users. Master Keyword Research Keyword research is the cornerstone of SEO. It’s the process of finding the search terms your ideal customers are using. A modern approach goes beyond just looking at search volume. It considers searcher intent (what someone really wants), keyword difficulty, and business relevance. Remember, nearly 74% of all search queries are long tail, meaning they consist of three or more words. These longer, more specific phrases often have lower search volume but much higher conversion rates because they signal a user is further along in their buying journey. A good seo guide for B2B must emphasize finding these high value queries. Map Everything to Searcher Intent Targeting a keyword isn’t enough; you must satisfy the why behind the search. Search intent mapping is the process of aligning your content with the user’s goal. The main intents are: Informational keywords : The user wants to learn something (e.g., “how to reduce customer churn”). Commercial: The user is researching solutions (e.g., “best crm for healthcare”). Transactional: The user is ready to act (e.g., “hubspot pricing”). Google is incredibly good at understanding intent. If you create a product page (transactional) to target an informational query, it probably won’t rank. Look at the current search results for a keyword. Are they blog posts, comparison guides, or product pages? That’s your clue. Matching intent leads to lower bounce rates and higher user satisfaction, which are powerful ranking signals. Part 2: Creating Content That Converts and Commands Authority With a solid strategy in place, it’s time to create the content that will attract and engage your audience. This section of our SEO guide for B2B focuses on building a content engine that establishes expertise and guides prospects through the funnel. Organize with Topic Clusters and Pillar Content A topic cluster is a modern way to organize your content to signal expertise. It involves creating a central “pillar” page on a broad topic (like an ultimate guide) and then surrounding it with multiple “cluster” pages that dive deep into related subtopics. For example, your pillar could be “The Ultimate Guide to Email Marketing,” with cluster posts on “Subject Line Best Practices” and “Email Automation Workflows.” Each cluster piece links back to the pillar, creating a tightly organized content hub. This structure helps search engines see your site as an authority on the entire topic, which can boost rankings for all related pages. Build a Funnel Aligned Content Library Funnel aligned content means creating assets for every stage of the buyer’s journey: top (awareness), middle (consideration), and bottom (decision). A potential customer needs different information as they move from identifying a problem to choosing a vendor. Consider that 47% of B2B buyers consume 3 to 5 pieces of content before ever speaking to a salesperson. Your job is to provide that content. Top of Funnel (TOFU): Attract a broad audience with blog posts, infographics, and ebooks. Middle of Funnel (MOFU): Nurture leads with webinars, case studies, and comparison guides. Bottom of Funnel (BOFU): Convert prospects with demos, free trials, and detailed product pages. Leverage a Long Tail Keyword Strategy A long tail keyword strategy focuses on those longer, highly specific search phrases we mentioned earlier. While a broad term like “CRM software” is incredibly competitive, a long tail query like “cloud crm software for small real estate teams” is much less so. More importantly, the person searching that phrase has a very specific need and is likely a high quality lead. These long tail queries make up the vast majority of all searches and their conversion rates are significantly higher. Creating niche blog posts and FAQ pages that answer these specific questions is a powerful way to attract qualified traffic. Craft Conversion Focused Content Every piece of content should have a purpose. Conversion focused content is designed not just to inform, but to guide the reader toward a specific action, like requesting a demo, downloading a whitepaper, or signing up for a trial. This type of content strategically includes persuasive elements and clear calls to action (CTAs). Remember, 75% of B2B buyers say the winning vendor’s content had a significant impact on their decision. By creating content that directly addresses pain points and presents your solution compellingly, you turn readers into revenue. Winning the Zero-Click Search As search engines provide more answers directly on the results page, your goal is to become the Featured Entity . Definitions: Use H3 headers for "What is [Industry Term]?" followed by a concise 40-word definition. Bulletized Lists: Use lists for "Step-by-Step" processes or "Top 5 Benefits." Google and AI agents favor these for snippet extraction. Unique Data: Publish proprietary benchmarks. If you own the data, AI models must cite your site as the origin, driving high-authority traffic even if total click volume drops. Become a Thought Leader Thought leadership means publishing authoritative, insightful content that positions your brand as an expert. This isn’t about chasing keywords; it’s about shaping the conversation in your industry. Think original research, strong opinion pieces, or visionary guides. This type of content is SEO gold because it naturally attracts high quality backlinks and social shares. According to a LinkedIn study, 58% of decision makers said that thought leadership directly led them to award business to a company. It builds trust and authority, which aligns perfectly with Google’s E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trust) guidelines. Part 3: Mastering On Site and Technical Optimization You can have the best content in the world, but if your website is slow, confusing, or broken, your SEO efforts will fail. This part of the SEO guide for B2B covers the critical on site optimizations that make your website a winner for both search engines and users. Perfect Your On Page SEO On page SEO involves optimizing individual page elements to improve rankings. For a step-by-step walkthrough, see our on-page SEO checklist . Key elements include: Title Tags: The clickable headline in search results. Make it compelling and include your primary keyword. Meta Descriptions: The short summary under the title. While not a direct ranking factor, a good one boosts clicks. Headings (H1, H2, H3): These structure your content for readability and help search engines understand the page hierarchy. URL Structure: Use short, clean, descriptive URLs. A URL containing a keyword has a 45% higher click through rate. Image Alt Text: Describe your images for accessibility and to give search engines more context. Nail Technical SEO Technical SEO is the work done “under the hood” to ensure search engines can crawl and index your site efficiently. If you’re not sure where to start, use this technical SEO audit guide . Key areas include: Site Speed: This is a critical ranking and user experience factor. A 1 second delay in mobile page load can reduce conversions by up to 20%. Mobile Friendliness: With Google’s mobile first indexing, your site must work flawlessly on mobile devices. Crawlability: Use a clean site structure, an XML sitemap, and a correct robots.txt file to help search engines find all your important pages. Security (HTTPS): A secure site is a must have. It’s a minor ranking signal and a major trust signal for users. Implement a Smart Internal Link Strategy Internal links are links from one page on your site to another. If you’re wondering about optimal counts, see this guide on how many internal links per page . A smart internal linking strategy helps users discover more of your content and helps search engines understand your site’s structure and which pages are most important. Adding a few relevant internal links from high authority pages on your site to a new page can give it an immediate ranking boost. It’s one of the most powerful and underutilized tactics in this SEO guide for B2B. Continuously Optimize Your Content Content optimization is the process of improving existing content to make it more search friendly and user friendly. This can involve updating information, improving readability, adding new keywords, or embedding multimedia. The average top 10 Google article is about 1,447 words long, indicating that comprehensive content often performs best. Don’t just publish and forget; regularly review and enhance your content. Refresh Old Content for a Traffic Boost A content refresh involves updating and republishing older posts. Over time, content can become outdated and lose traffic. Refreshing it with new stats, insights, and examples can bring it back to life. HubSpot found that updating old blog posts can increase their organic traffic by as much as 106%. This is one of the highest ROI activities in SEO. For a startup or SMB, a service that continuously rewrites underperforming pages, like the one offered by Rankai , can be a game changer for maintaining momentum. Optimize Your Product Pages For B2B SaaS or e commerce companies, product pages are where the magic happens. Product page optimization involves using descriptive titles, writing unique and benefit focused descriptions, using high quality images with alt text, and encouraging customer reviews. Including structured data (schema markup) can also help you get rich snippets like star ratings in search results, which can dramatically increase click through rates. How to Optimize for AI Overviews and Chatbots By 2026, nearly 95% of B2B buying journeys begin within a large language model or AI-powered search. To ensure your brand is cited as a source in these summaries, follow the S.T.A.R. framework: S - Structured Data: Implement comprehensive Schema markup (Organization, Product, and FAQ) so AI agents can parse your facts without ambiguity. T - Transparent Sourcing: Cite original research and verified data. AI models prioritize "citation-worthy" content that isn't just a rehash of existing web text. A - Answer-First Formatting: Place direct, 1-3 sentence answers to complex industry questions at the very top of your sub-sections. R - Real-World Proof: Incorporate case studies and "Experience" signals. AI systems are increasingly trained to distinguish between generic AI-generated filler and firsthand professional insight. Part 4: Building Authority and Measuring Success Getting your website and content in order is half the battle. The other half is building a strong reputation across the web and meticulously tracking your results to prove ROI. Build Authority with Quality Link Building Link building is the process of acquiring hyperlinks from other websites to your own. These links, or backlinks, act as “votes of confidence” and are a major Google ranking factor. The key is quality over quantity. A single backlink from a high authority website is more valuable than many from low quality sites. Pages ranking #1 on Google have, on average, 3.8 times more backlinks than those ranking in positions #2 through #10. To build links, you can create link worthy content (like original research), engage in digital PR, or guest post on relevant industry blogs. This is a core pillar of authority building, which is about increasing your website’s overall credibility in the eyes of search engines. A strong backlink profile makes your entire site more resilient and more likely to rank for competitive terms. Track Your SEO KPI Measurement You can’t improve what you don’t measure. SEO KPI (Key Performance Indicator) measurement is how you track success and justify your investment. Key metrics to watch include: Organic Traffic: The number of visitors from search. Keyword Rankings: Your position for target keywords. Click Through Rate (CTR): The percentage of people who click your result. Conversion Rate: The percentage of organic visitors who become leads. Organic Revenue: The sales generated from organic search. Focusing on the right KPIs is a vital part of this SEO guide for B2B. While traffic is great, leads and revenue are what really matter to the business. Understand Attribution Modeling The B2B buyer journey is rarely linear. A prospect might first find your blog via organic search, later see a social media ad, and finally convert after clicking an email link. Attribution modeling is the method of assigning credit to these different touchpoints. Instead of a simple “last click” model, many companies use multi touch models to understand how different channels, including SEO, contribute to the final sale. This ensures SEO gets credit for its crucial role early in the funnel. Combine SEO with CRO CRO, or Conversion Rate Optimization, is the practice of improving your website to convert more visitors into customers. Combining CRO with SEO is a powerhouse move. You’ve worked hard to get organic traffic; now make sure your landing pages are optimized to capture those leads. Simple changes like improving page speed, simplifying forms, or testing different CTAs can have a huge impact. Remember, SEO leads have a 14.6% close rate, compared to just 1.7% for outbound leads. Optimizing for conversions maximizes the value of that high quality traffic. Part 5: Navigating the Future with AI The world of search is changing rapidly, driven by artificial intelligence. A modern SEO guide for B2B must address how to adapt to this new landscape. Understand AI Overview Impact AI Overviews are the AI generated summaries that now appear at the top of many Google search results. This has a massive impact on SEO. On the one hand, roughly 60% of all searches now result in no click to any website, as users get their answers directly on the results page. This is a challenge. On the other hand, companies are adapting; nearly 70% of businesses report higher ROI after integrating AI into their SEO workflows. The game is no longer just about ranking; it’s about being visible within these new AI powered features. Embrace Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is the new practice of optimizing your content to be cited and featured within these AI answers. The goal is to become a trusted source for the AI. While it may lead to fewer direct clicks, being cited in an AI overview can increase a page’s click through by 35% because it establishes your brand as the authority. Strategies for GEO include using clear, factual language, structuring content with schema markup, and building overall domain authority. It’s about ensuring your content is so clear and trustworthy that the AI chooses you. This is a complex, fast moving space. Working with an agile team that blends AI tools with human experts, like the monthly service from Rankai , can help you stay ahead of the curve and adapt your strategy as search evolves. Frequently Asked Questions What is the first step in a B2B SEO strategy? The first step is always deep audience research. Before you do anything else, you must identify your target audience and develop detailed buyer personas. This foundational work informs every subsequent decision in your SEO strategy, from keyword selection to content creation. How is B2B SEO different from B2C SEO? B2B SEO typically involves a much smaller, more specialized audience with a longer and more complex sales cycle. The focus is on generating qualified leads rather than driving a large volume of direct sales. Content is often more technical and informational, aimed at solving specific business problems for a buying committee, not an individual consumer. This makes a tailored seo guide for B2B essential. How long does it take for B2B SEO to show results? SEO is a long term strategy. While you might see some quick wins from technical fixes, it generally takes 4 to 12 months to see significant results in terms of traffic and lead generation. Consistency in content creation and authority building is key to achieving and maintaining rankings. What are the most important KPIs for a B2B SEO campaign? While organic traffic and keyword rankings are important, the most critical KPIs for B2B are business focused. These include Marketing Qualified Leads (MQLs) from organic search, organic lead conversion rate, and ultimately, the pipeline and revenue generated from the SEO channel. Is link building still important for B2B SEO? Absolutely. High quality backlinks from relevant, authoritative websites remain one of the strongest ranking signals for Google. For B2B companies, earning links from industry publications, partners, and respected blogs is a powerful way to build credibility and improve search visibility. How does AI change the approach in this seo guide for B2B? AI changes the game in two ways. First, tools can be used to scale content creation and keyword research. Second, the rise of AI Overviews in search results requires a new strategy called Generative Engine Optimization (GEO). The focus is now shifting from just ranking in the top 10 to also being the trusted source cited within AI answers.

title: Guide to AI-powered segmentation for subscribers
summary: Guide to AI-powered segmentation for subscribers. Understand behavioral signals, identify at-risk users, and take action across the subscription lifecycle.
body_text: Segmentation in subscription businesses often begins with lists built around plan type, tenure, or recent activity. These structures help organize a subscriber base, but they provide limited guidance when it comes to deciding what action to take next. The limitation becomes clear in execution, for example, two subscribers can fall into the same segment and still require entirely different interventions. One may be approaching an upgrade moment, while another may be moving toward churn. This kind of difference is not visible in static groupings. What tends to matter more is how behavior changes over time. Patterns in usage, engagement, and billing often indicate where a subscriber is heading before outcomes such as churn or expansion become explicit. AI-powered segmentation builds on this by grouping subscribers according to those patterns. The result is a set of audiences that map more directly to lifecycle decisions, making it easier to determine where to intervene and what to test. Customer segmentation in a subscription context Customer segmentation refers to the process of dividing a subscriber base into groups so that each group can be managed differently. Traditional approaches rely on attributes such as plan type, subscription length, or acquisition channel. These attributes are useful for structuring communication and reporting, but they do not capture how subscribers behave after signing up. Behavior-based segmentation focuses instead on how subscribers interact with the product. It looks at frequency of use, depth of engagement, and changes in usage patterns over time. This makes it possible to group subscribers based on how they are progressing through the lifecycle rather than where they started. Limitations of rule-based segmentation Rule-based segmentation is straightforward to implement and easy to maintain. It typically relies on conditions such as inactivity over a fixed period or time spent on a particular plan. The challenge lies in how these rules are interpreted. Subscribers who meet the same condition may be moving in different directions. One may return to regular usage, while another may continue to disengage. Static segments do not account for this variation. They capture a moment, but not the trajectory leading up to it. As a result, they provide limited guidance when deciding how to respond. Segmentation becomes more effective when it reflects how behavior is evolving, not just what has already happened. AI-powered segmentation evaluation signals AI-powered segmentation brings together multiple data signals and evaluates how they interact over time. In most subscription businesses, these signals include: Engagement data : How often a subscriber uses the product, which features they use, how deeply they engage per session, and whether that engagement is trending up or down over time. Billing behavior : Payment history, plan changes, whether they've ever paused or requested a refund, and how they responded to price changes. Acquisition context : How they found you, what offer they signed up on, and which channel brought them in. Subscribers acquired via a promotional discount often have a very different lifetime trajectory than those who signed up at full price. Support interactions : Whether they've contacted support, what they asked about, and how those interactions resolved. A subscriber who asked how to cancel three months ago is a very different risk profile from one who asked how to upgrade. Content or feature affinity : In media and SaaS subscriptions, especially, which specific content or features a subscriber gravitates toward tells you a great deal about where their value perception is anchored. Each of these provides a partial view of subscriber behavior. The value comes from combining them. Patterns begin to emerge when changes in usage are viewed alongside billing behavior or when engagement trends are considered in relation to acquisition source. These patterns make it possible to identify groups of subscribers who share similar trajectories, such as those gradually disengaging or those increasing their level of usage. Segmentation then shifts from describing subscribers to identifying where they are likely to move next. Segmentation in practice Segmentation becomes useful when it is directly connected to action. Each audience should correspond to a specific decision or intervention. A practical structure follows a simple sequence: Define the segment Apply an action Measure the outcome Refine based on results Over time, this creates a system in which segmentation informs ongoing lifecycle management rather than remaining a static classification. Example 1: Declining engagement A common and high-impact segment consists of subscribers whose usage is trending downward over time. This pattern typically appears before churn becomes visible in reporting. These subscribers tend to visit less frequently, engage with fewer features or content, and show a gradual reduction in activity. Learn how a streaming media company was able to boost engagement by +23% using Subsets Actions for this segment focus on restoring engagement in a targeted way, for example: Re-engagement campaigns can be based on the subscriber’s past usage, guiding them back to familiar actions rather than introducing new ones. Product prompts can be triggered when usage drops, directing attention toward features that deliver clear value. Content or feature recommendations can also be tailored to previous behavior so that the next step feels relevant and easy to take. Example 2: Trials not activated Another important segment includes trial users who have not reached a meaningful activation point. These users have signed up but have not experienced the core value of the product. This is often reflected in limited engagement and incomplete onboarding. Actions here focus on extending the window for value realization. These can include: Extending the trial period for low-engagement users provides more time to reach activation before a payment decision is required. Onboarding flows can be adjusted to emphasize one clear outcome, reducing complexity and guiding users toward the most important actions. Guided product experiences can also help users complete key steps without relying on self-directed exploration. Example 3: Interest lost mid-lifecycle Some subscribers remain active in billing while gradually reducing their level of engagement. This segment is often overlooked because revenue continues, even as usage declines. These subscribers show fewer sessions, reduced depth of interaction, and lower usage of key features over time. Actions for this group focus on reinforcing value before disengagement deepens, which can include: Feature highlights can reintroduce parts of the product that have not yet been explored. Personalized recommendations can align with past behavior to maintain relevance. Lifecycle messaging can also be timed to periods of declining engagement, encouraging a return to meaningful usage. Example 4: Highly engaged subscribers Segmentation also identifies subscribers who are strong candidates for expansion. These users engage consistently, use core features deeply, and often show signs of approaching the limits of their current plan. Actions for this group are centered on growth, such as: Upgrade prompts can be introduced at moments when usage indicates readiness, ensuring that the timing aligns with perceived value. Premium features can be surfaced within the product experience, allowing subscribers to see their benefits before making a decision. Pricing experiments can also be applied to understand which upgrade paths lead to sustained engagement after conversion. Example 5: At risk of cancelling/churn Another key segment includes subscribers who show early signs of cancellation risk. These signals may include declining engagement, billing-related friction, or changes in renewal behavior. Actions in this case focus on maintaining the relationship, which can include: Downgrade options can be introduced to allow subscribers to continue at a lower level of commitment. Targeted retention offers can be aligned with how the subscriber has used the product rather than applied broadly. Prompts to update payment details or restore renewal settings can also address friction before it leads to a failed renewal. Where to start & common mistakes Starting with a single segment, typically one with clear retention impact, allows teams to define a specific action and measure its effect. From there, additional segments and interventions can be introduced gradually. Segments should update continuously as subscriber behavior changes, ensuring that actions remain relevant over time. A focused approach is more effective than attempting to build a complete system at once. Several patterns tend to reduce the effectiveness of segmentation. Segmentation performs best when it reflects real-life usage patterns and is maintained as an ongoing process. Treating surface-level activity as a measure of value can lead to misleading conclusions. Creating too many segments early on can make execution difficult without improving outcomes. Leaving segments unchanged over time reduces their relevance as subscriber behavior evolves. Acting on segments without understanding the underlying behavior can also limit the effectiveness of interventions. Conclusion AI-powered segmentation allows subscription teams to work with how subscribers actually behave across the lifecycle. When segmentation is connected to action, testing, and measurement, it becomes part of a continuous system that improves over time. Audiences evolve as behavior changes, and interventions become more precise through iteration. title: NuScale Power and Ebara Elliott Energy Announce a Strategic Partnership to Showcase Use of Advanced Nuclear Technology to Power Petrochemical Plants
summary: NuScale & Ebara Elliott Energy announced a collaborative research program to field test a commercial scale high-temperature steam compressor to integrate NuScale Power Modules™ with petrochemical plants needing process heat.
body_text: Collaboration Examines the Development, Demonstration and Field Testing of an Industrial Scale Steam Compressor Using NuScale Power Modules™ Partnership to be Highlighted at upcoming World Petrochemical Conference in Houston, TX CORVALLIS, Ore . – NuScale Power Corporation (NYSE: SMR) (NuScale), the industry-leading provider of proprietary and innovative advanced small modular reactor (SMR) nuclear technology, and Ebara Elliott Energy (EEE), a global leading producer of advanced turbomachinery solutions, announced a collaborative research program to demonstrate and field test a commercial scale high-temperature steam compressor to integrate NuScale Power Modules™ (NPM) with petrochemical plants needing process heat. EEE’s compressors, turbines and pumps are based on proven technology, relying on more than 100 years of operational experience and thousands of units operating around the globe in chemical facilities 24/7. NuScale’s technology, powered by its innovative NPM, is the first and only SMR to have received U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission design approval. Under the program, EEE and NuScale will collaborate to support the development, manufacturing, and integration of critical turbomachinery and energy-conversion systems for petrochemical plants powered by NuScale technology. The collaboration is intended to combine NuScale’s industry-leading SMR technology with EEE’s decades of expertise in steam turbines, compressors, and rotating equipment to deliver clean, proven and efficient nuclear power solutions for the petrochemical plants, a first for the industry. NPMs are designed to produce reliable process steam for industrial applications at 500oC or higher, a temperature previously considered beyond the reach of light water reactors. Steam produced by the NPM will be isolated from outside facilities via an intermediate heat exchanger and subsequently raised to high temperature through the simple process of adiabatic compression. “The application of NuScale’s industry-leading technology to produce high temperature process steam is an exciting use case that unlocks significant commercial opportunities for petrochemical plants, and we are proud to partner with EEE to deliver these high-performance energy solutions to customers worldwide” said Dr. José Reyes, Chief Technology Officer of NuScale Power. “Not only does our collaboration with EEE strengthen NuScale’s robust supply chain, but their deep experience in turbomachinery and manufacturing excellence also aligns perfectly with our mission to provide safe, scalable, and carbon-free energy.” “This partnership leverages our century of engineering excellence to accelerate the deployment of NuScale’s innovative clean energy technology,” said Ron Josefczyk, Vice President, New Apparatus, Ebara Elliott Energy. “By combining our specialized design and manufacturing capabilities with NuScale’s SMR design, we are creating a reliable, low-carbon power solution specifically optimized for the rigorous demands of the global petrochemical industry.” The project is in progress with the compressor target completion in 2027. Currently, the partners are seeking candidates for the next phase of the project, field testing. NuScale and Ebara Elliott Energy will gather in Houston next week to share the progress of this important collaboration at the World Petrochemical Conference, where Chief Technology Officer Dr. José Reyes will deliver a presentation titled “Reframing Nuclear Heat: From Future Concept to Commercial Reality” on March 24. NuScale and EEE will also be welcoming conference attendees to their booth in the foyer of the Marriott Marquis Houston where visitors can learn more. About NuScale Power Founded in 2007, NuScale Power Corporation (NYSE: SMR) is the industry-leading provider of proprietary and innovative advanced small modular reactor (SMR) nuclear technology, with a mission to help power the global energy transition by delivering safe, scalable, and reliable carbon-free energy. The Company’s groundbreaking SMR technology is powered by the NuScale Power Module™, a small, safe, pressurized water reactor that can each generate 77 megawatts of electricity (MWe) or 250 megawatts thermal (gross), and can be scaled to meet customer needs through an array of flexible configurations up to 924 MWe (12 modules) of output. As the first and only SMR to have its designs certified by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, NuScale is well-positioned to serve diverse customers across the world by supplying nuclear energy for electrical generation, data centers, district heating, desalination, commercial-scale hydrogen production, and other process heat applications. About Ebara Elliott Energy A solution provider in the energy industry, Ebara Elliott Energy (EEE) designs, manufactures, and services technically advanced centrifugal and axial compressors, steam turbines, power recovery expanders, custom pumps, and cryogenic products used in the petrochemical, refining, oil & gas, and liquefied gas industries, as well as in power applications. EEE’s 29 globally distributed service and sales centers provide skillful and effective support for these products. Ebara Elliott Energy employs 3,700 people around the world.
